(point 6) Microprocessors brought computing power to a single piece of silicon. (point 7) Personal computers moved computing from labs into homes and offices. (point 8) The internet connected computers worldwide into a single network. (point 9) Smartphones put a powerful computer into nearly everyone's pocket. (point 10) Cloud computing moved workloads off individual machines entirely. (point 11) Machine learning models now run on specialized accelerator hardware. An overview of the water cycle. The sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, causing evaporation. (point 1) Water vapor rises into the atmosphere and cools as it ascends. (point 2) Cooled vapor condenses around particles to form clouds. (point 3) Clouds grow until droplets are heavy enough to fall as precipitation. (point 4) Rain and snow return water to the surface of the earth. (point 5) Some precipitation soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. (point 6) Groundwater slowly flows underground until it reaches a river or sea. (point 7) Surface runoff carries water across land back into larger bodies. (point 8) Plants absorb groundwater through roots and release vapor via leaves. (point 9) This release of vapor from plants is called transpiration. (point 10) Ice caps and glaciers store water as solid ice for long periods. (point 11) Eventually that stored ice melts and rejoins the cycle as liquid water. An overview of an overview of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in plants. (point 1) Chlorophyll inside chloroplasts absorbs light, mostly red and blue. (point 2) Water molecules are split apart during the light-dependent reactions. (point 3) Splitting water releases oxygen as a byproduct into the atmosphere. (point 4) Light reactions produce energy carriers used later in the process. (point 5) The Calvin cycle uses that energy to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. (point 6) Stomata are small pores that let carbon dioxide into the leaf. (point 7) The same pores also allow water vapor to escape through transpiration. (point 8) Glucose produced by photosynthesis fuels the plant's growth. (point 9) Excess sugar can be stored as starch for later use. (point 10) Photosynthesis is the foundation of nearly every food chain on Earth. (point 11) Without it, most life as we know it could not be sustained. An overview of the history of the printing press. Movable type printing was independently developed in East Asia first. (point 1) Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press using metal movable type. (point 2) His press combined oil-based ink, a screw mechanism, and metal type. (point 3) The Gutenberg Bible was among the first major books printed this way. (point 4) Printed books became far cheaper to produce than hand-copied ones. (point 5) Literacy rates rose as books became more affordable and available. (point 6) The press helped spread scientific and religious ideas quickly. (point 7) Standardized spelling became more common once texts were printed. (point 8) Newspapers eventually grew out of the same printing technology. (point 9) Steam-powered presses later increased printing speed enormously. (point 10) Offset printing became the dominant technique in the 20th century. (point 11) Digital publishing has since changed how most text reaches readers. An overview of how compilers work. A compiler translates source code written by a programmer into machine code. (point 1) Lexical analysis breaks source text into a stream of tokens. (point 2) Parsing arranges those tokens into a tree that reflects the grammar. (point 3) Semantic analysis checks that the parsed program actually makes sense. (point 4) Type checking is one common part of semantic analysis. (point 5) An intermediate representation lets the compiler reason about the program. (point 6) Optimization passes rewrite that representation to run faster. (point 7) Register allocation decides which values live in fast hardware registers. (point 8) Code generation produces the final machine instructions. (point 9) Linking combines compiled pieces into a single runnable program. (point 10) Just-in-time compilers perform some of these steps while a program runs. (point 11) Interpreters skip ahead-of-time compilation and execute source directly. An overview of basics of network protocols. A network protocol is an agreed set of rules for exchanging data. (point 1) The Internet Protocol addresses and routes packets between machines. (point 2) TCP adds reliability on top of IP by retransmitting lost packets. (point 3) UDP skips that reliability to minimize latency for some workloads. (point 4) DNS translates human-readable names into numeric IP addresses. (point 5) HTTP is the application protocol underlying most web traffic. (point 6) TLS encrypts a connection so eavesdroppers cannot read the contents. (point 7) A handshake establishes shared parameters before data flows. (point 8) Routers forward packets toward their destination hop by hop. (point 9) Firewalls inspect traffic and decide whether to allow it through. (point 10) Load balancers spread incoming requests across many servers. (point 11) Together these layers let two distant machines talk reliably. An overview of an overview of plate tectonics. The Earth's crust is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. (point 1) These plates float on a slowly flowing layer of the mantle below. (point 2) Plates can move apart, collide, or slide past one another. (point 3) Divergent boundaries form where plates move apart from each other. (point 4) New crust forms at divergent boundaries as magma rises upward. (point 5) Convergent boundaries form where plates push together. (point 6) One plate often sinks beneath another at a convergent boundary. (point 7) This sinking process is called subduction. (point 8) Transform boundaries occur where plates slide past each other. (point 9) Earthquakes are common along all three types of plate boundary. (point 10) Volcanoes often form near subduction zones and divergent boundaries. An overview of an overview of distributed systems. A distributed system is a collection of machines that act as one. (point 1) Network delays and partial failures are a normal part of life here. (point 2) The CAP theorem describes a tradeoff between consistency and availability. (point 3) Consensus protocols let machines agree on a single value despite failures. (point 4) Replication copies data across machines to survive individual failures. (point 5) Sharding splits data across machines to spread load evenly. (point 6) Leader election picks one machine to coordinate a group temporarily. (point 7) Idempotent operations can be safely retried after a timeout. (point 8) Clock skew between machines complicates reasoning about ordering. (point 9) Logical clocks give a consistent notion of ordering without real time. (point 10) Observability tools help operators understand a system under load. (point 11) Good distributed systems degrade gracefully instead of failing all at once.
